For generations, the festival has rested on a simple and enduring aspiration: to preserve value today and build financial security for tomorrow. Physical gold has held a sacred place in this tradition because it joins cultural meaning with a dependable store of value. For earlier generations, the ritual meant a visit to the local jeweller, a purchase of bullion or jewellery, and a place in the home safe or bank locker. It was familiar, but it carried friction: making charges, storage and insurance costs, and the ever-present risk of loss or theft. The aspiration endures. Its expression is changing. Millennials and Gen Z grew up with digital payments and app-based services, and they expect buying an asset to be as seamless as booking a ride. Importantly, the shift is additive rather than substitutive. Many younger investors still buy gold, but increasingly through gold ETFs and mutual funds, which remove making charges and storage worries. Alongside this, digital platforms have opened equities, mutual funds and digital assets to anyone who can invest a modest sum each month. Also Read | Dhanteras 2026: Buying gold today? Here's how to choose between jewellery, coins, ETFs and SGBs The more consequential change is one of mindset. The question is moving from “what should I buy this Dhanteras?” to “how should my assets work together?” Diversification, asset allocation , time horizon and position sizing shape long-term outcomes far more than the timing of any single purchase. A monthly systematic investment across gold, equity and other asset classes builds exposure steadily. Within such a framework, newer assets are best seen as a small satellite allocation around a diversified core. Live Events Bitcoin has often been the first step into this ecosystem. Its decentralised network, fixed supply of 21 million coins and high divisibility explain why it is called digital gold . The comparison is useful but imperfect. Gold’s value rests on thousands of years of cultural consensus and broad jewellery and industrial demand. Bitcoin is about fifteen years old, and its price volatility is considerably higher. India's gold demand fell 29% year-on-year to 162.5 tonnes in the July–September quarter, according to the World Gold Council. Yet the value of that demand rose 3% to Rs 2,419 billion, because domestic prices averaged Rs 148,891 per 10 grams, up 45% from a year earlier. In other words, Indians bought considerably less gold by volume but continued to spend more on it. ETMarkets.com Markets regulator Sebi on Monday reduced the cooling-off period for offer-for-sale (OFS) transactions by privately placed illiquid infrastructure investment trusts (InvITs) to 8 weeks from 12 weeks earlier. At present, the cooling-off period for transactions - purchases or sales before and after an OFS - is based on liquidity. It stands at two weeks for the most liquid shares, four weeks for liquid shares and 12 weeks for illiquid shares. In an order passed on Tuesday, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) imposed a penalty of Rs 10 lakh each on Woodstock Broking and its director Suresh Kanmal Jajoo and Marfatia Stock Broking and its director Nishil Surendra Marfatia. The order relates to a Sebi investigation with respect to trades executed by certain entities, which appeared to be in the nature of front-running of the trades of Axis Mutual Fund (Big Client), pursuant to certain alerts generated by the surveillance system. The investigation period was from April 1, 2021 to March 31, 2022. Sebi found that the two brokers facilitated the installation and operation of their ODIN trading terminals on a computer system used by Prijesh Kurani in Dubai, who was neither an authorised person nor a registered dealer of the brokers. In Marfatia's case, the market watchdog relied on a statement from its managing director, Nishil Marfatia; WhatsApp conversations involving its IT personnel; and common MAC IDs linking the trading systems used for transactions routed through the two brokers. The regulator held that the brokers aided the execution of fraudulent trades by providing the necessary infrastructure and technical assistance, in violation of the Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices (PFUTP) Rules. Agencies Markets regulator Sebi on Wednesday relaxed the Know Your Customer (KYC) requirements for individual persons resident outside India, including Non-Resident Indians (NRIs), Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs) and foreign nationals, allowing them to complete the onboarding process digitally. They can now complete the process from Financial Action Task Force (FATF)-compliant countries without being physically present in India. The revised framework will come into effect from December 3, Sebi said in its circular. Under the framework, intermediaries registered with Sebi can accept digital submission of KYC information and supporting documents from such clients without requiring them to be physically present in India during the onboarding process. The move is aimed at simplifying the onboarding process and easing compliance requirements for overseas investors. Live Events "In order to ease the process of onboarding an individual Person Resident Outside India (PROI) client, it has been decided to review the existing provisions governing the KYC process. Individual PROI client shall mean a Non-Resident Indian (NRI), Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) or foreign national," SEBI said. "The requirement of a client being in India during digital onboarding is being relaxed for an individual PROI client located in a FATF-compliant country, and the intermediary may accept digital submission of KYC information and supporting documents from such client," it added. The regulator has also introduced greater portability of KYC records, directing KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs) to tag individual attributes as 'validated' wherever they have been verified against official or source databases. KYC records will remain portable and can be shared with other intermediaries, irrespective of whether every individual attribute has been validated. Further, intermediaries will be permitted to rely on KYC undertaken by another SEBI-registered intermediary or an entity regulated by other financial sector regulators, based on records available with KRAs or the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCRR). However, the intermediary will retain ultimate responsibility for ensuring KYC compliance , including undertaking enhanced due diligence based on the client's risk profile. ANI Capital markets regulator Sebi has allowed domestic and foreign portfolio investors to take positions of up to USD 5 million in currency derivatives contracts without having to establish an underlying exposure. In a circular on Thursday, Sebi revised norms aligned with the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) October 10 circular, which changed the threshold for taking positions in foreign exchange derivatives involving the rupee without establishing an underlying exposure. Under the revised framework, domestic clients and foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) can take long or short positions up to a single limit of USD 5 million equivalent of notional value (outstanding at any point), across all currency pairs involving the Indian rupee, put together, and combined across all recognised stock exchanges. The regulator has also specified that FPIs must ensure that their short positions across all contracts in foreign currency-rupee pairs do not exceed USD 5 million. For positions above the USD 5 million threshold, FPIs taking the long positions must have an underlying exposure in Indian debt or equity securities, including units of equity and debt mutual funds, Sebi said. Live Events Domestic clients can take positions beyond the limit subject to conditions specified by the RBI in its master direction on Risk Management and Inter-Bank Dealings dated October 10. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) said stock exchanges and clearing corporations must put in place systems to implement the revised provisions and make consequential amendments to their rules and regulations.
